title: Practical tactics to build reliable AI apps — Dmitry Kuchin, Multinear
talk_summary: Dmitry Kuchin argues that reliable AI apps come from building task-specific evals first (reverse-engineered from real user scenarios and source materials), then iterating via experimentation against that benchmark. He rejects abstract data-science metrics (factuality, groundedness) in favor of concrete, per-question checklists that reveal why a case fails and catch regressions.

takeaways.what_they_do: Use a strong LLM to reverse-engineer, from the source docs/materials, both the user questions and the specific checklist criteria an answer must satisfy; build these before or alongside the first solution version.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you build your evals not at the end of the process but in the very beginning of the process

takeaways.technique: Per-case checklists instead of aggregate scores
takeaways.what_they_do: Define very specific criteria per question (e.g. must mention SMS validation and the no-mobile fallback) so a failing case tells you exactly what is wrong, rather than averaging into a single number.
takeaways.evidence_quote: you need to be very specific about what exact information you need to see in the answer

takeaways.what_they_do: Generate ~50 variations of the same question across different personas to confirm the solution still passes the same checklist regardless of phrasing.
takeaways.evidence_quote: generate like 50 different variations of the same question and see if I still get the right answer

takeaways.technique: Frequent eval runs to catch regressions
takeaways.what_they_do: Run the eval benchmark on every change because prompt/logic/model tweaks frequently fix one case and silently break another.
Once a stable eval baseline exists, use it to test cheaper models or simpler approaches (e.g. 4o-mini vs 4o, graph RAG vs simpler logic) and only adopt if the benchmark holds.
Match eval style to task: LLM-as-judge for support bots, mock DB with known schema/data for text-to-SQL, simple rubric match for classifiers, plus explicit guardrail cases for out-of-scope questions.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the evaluations that you need to build ... are completely different depending on the solution
